newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya's Moi says fully embraces reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kenya's Moi says fully embraces reforms.

text.p: Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi said on Friday that he fully embraced constitutional reforms and a "minimum" package from his ruling KANU party would be debated and approved in the current session of parliament.
Leaders of a Kenyan political reform campaign, which has seen violent clashes between police and demonstrators, urged supporters not to abandon a crusade for change.

"These people (opposition-backed alliance) have been asking for (minimum constitutional) reforms. I have agreed, I have agreed fully. Parliament will debate and enact them," Moi told a rally in Molo in his native Rift Valley Province.

"After these, a commission will follow that will review the entire constitution. I have always said there was a need for changes in our constitution. Changes that will make the lives of all Kenyans better," added Moi in comments relayed by the state Kenya Broadcasting Corporation television.
KANU on Thursday proposed measures that could effectively pull the reform rug from under an opposition-backed alliance, which had forged rare unity among opponents of President Moi.
The proposals surprised opposition leaders and stunned many ordinary Kenyans, the backbone since June of rallies and clashes with riot police that hit tourism and scared foreign investors.

"They (KANU) have dented the pressure," admitted Willy Mutunga, a leader of an alliance of opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies campaigning for reforms before elections this year. "It's up to us to make the next move."
But parliamentary opposition leader Michael Kijana Wamalwa urged opposition leaders to pursue the path of dialogue and meet government representatives over KANU's "minimum package".

"KANU has answered the question of whether it wants reforms with a minimum package of its own. Now, those in the opposition have to join in the dialogue and discuss the exact nature of constitutional reforms that go to parliament," Wamalwa told a news conference in the capital.
Moi and Wamalwa said Kenyans must embrace dialogue to avoid any further violence or loss of life.
Opposition leaders earlier urged 400 supporters at an open-air service for the dead from clashes this month to stick to the campaign they hoped would unseat the 73-year-old Moi.

"Moi is now acting out of weakness. Moi will not beat us. We will win ... When we fight for change we don't want Moi to give it to us. We want to win it ourselves," James Orengo, the deputy opposition leader in parliament, told a cheering crowd.
Police remained out of sight as what was billed as a memorial service with the bodies of two of the dead in coffins at the feet of speakers turned at times into a political rally.

KANU's National Executive Council chaired by Moi proposed on Thursday parliament pass a bill for 11 controversial laws to be "repealed or amended where deemed necessary" before elections and to set up a commission to review Kenya's constitution.

If enacted by parliament, where KANU has a majority, the repeal of the 11 laws, some dating back to the colonial period, would reduce Moi's power. But it would also remove a main pillar of the reform drive and possibly split the opposition again.
Moi has been tipped to win another five-year term and could move to catch the opposition off guard, if it loses its common cause, by calling elections shortly after repealing the 11 laws.

Opposition FORD-Asili party chairman Kenneth Matiba in a statement accused Moi of using the tactics of "divide and rule" and said his party would only accept a constitutional conference and not "legal reforms which KANU is giving the country".
